1:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the plan of the whole. The prophecy against Tyre runs across three chapters and consists of four words of God, the first threatening the destruction of the city and state, the second a lamentation over that destruction, the third a threat against her king and the fourth a lamentation over his fall; Sidon gets only a short paragraph at the end, because the grandeur of Phoenicia was by then concentrated in Tyre, to which Sidon had lost the leadership. On the date, Gill and Wesley reckon the eleventh year as that in which Jerusalem was taken, Wesley placing the month after the capture. Ellicott is more careful: the month is not given and cannot now be ascertained, and though one recension of the Greek supplies the first month, its omission elsewhere makes that likely a conjecture, the loss being probably a scribal error.

Henry makes a distinction the others do not. The Tyrians, he says, did not hate Jerusalem as the Ammonites and Edomites did, nor were they spiteful or persecuting; they were men of business and wide acquaintance, and therefore not bigoted like narrow souls that live retired and never see the world. Their whole care was to get estates and enlarge trade, and they looked on Jerusalem not as an enemy but as a rival, an earlier king of theirs having been a friend to David and Solomon. Ellicott says the same at greater length: the exultation is purely selfish and commercial, showing nothing of the religious animosity charged against the nations of the previous chapter. He explains what was at stake, that Jerusalem had been the emporium of the inland trade from Arabia and even India and the broker between Egypt and the northern nations, so that a city so placed must have been the centre of transactions Tyre would gladly have monopolised.

How many conquests are foretold divides them. Clarke allows that the many nations may be the mixed provinces of the Chaldean empire and the soldiers of many nations in its army, but doubts it, and prefers the successive nations that fought against Tyre in later ages, noting that she was finally destroyed only in the sixteenth century of the Christian era. Ellicott agrees, and reads the prophet as glancing at the outset down the whole future history: not merely the conquest he will describe presently, but all the successive conquests until the city should be utterly desolate. The comparison is exact for the situation, he says, since God will bring nation after nation against Tyre as the sea throws wave after wave against her rock.

The scraping of the dust and the bare rock are pressed hardest. Clarke says plainly that this cannot refer to the capture by Nebuchadnezzar, since the city flourished long after his time. Ellicott adds the outcome, that the ruins of the ancient city have all been thrown into the sea and what remains is of mediaeval construction, most of which has itself been carried away. On the spreading of nets Gill collects travellers reports, one scholar recalling a learned man who had lived ten years in Syria and said that the ruins of Tyre, the rocks running to the sea and the stones made smooth by sun and wave and wind, used for nothing but drying the nets of fishermen, brought this passage to his mind. Ellicott confirms it for his own day, that a miserable village of three thousand has grown up on part of the site within the present century while other parts still have no more important use, and that the Tyre on the mainland has so utterly disappeared that its site cannot be identified. Clarke explains the two cities, one on the mainland soon taken and one on a rock in the sea that cost thirteen years of siege, which together formed one city and one state.
7:
Ellicott notes the spelling of the name, which is closer to the Babylonian form than the one the Hebrews finally adopted, and explains the two titles: king of kings because many countries were subject to him and their kings his vassals, and from the north because that was the direction from which his armies must approach, though Babylon itself lay south of Tyre in actual latitude. Clarke says the first title was an ancient one among the Asiatic despots and is still in use.

The siege works raise a problem, since the particulars are those of an attack on a mainland city. Ellicott answers it two ways: the old Tyre on the mainland was approached in the ordinary manner, and for the island the king must have contrived a bridge of boats or some other way across the shoal channel, which was then only twelve hundred yards wide. If he built a mole it was afterwards removed, since when Alexander built one two and a half centuries later sand accumulated on it until the island became a peninsula joined to the shore by a wide beach. Clarke reads the daughters in the field as the mainland city, since forts and mounts and chariots could not be brought against the other.

On the engines Gill reports that some took them for crossbows throwing stones or arrows and others for machines that beat down walls, and that some identify them with battering rams, a late invention which this prophet is said to be the first writer to mention. Ellicott agrees on the rams and adds that the axes of the English are in the original swords, either the specific put for the general or a hyperbole for the power of the swords of that army. He also corrects the strong garrisons: the word means a pillar set up as a monument, so that the sense is the pillars of thy strength, probably those an ancient historian describes as standing in the temple at Tyre, one of gold and the other of emerald. Wesley guesses at bastions or triumphal arches, and Gill calls the covering dust of the horses a hyperbole.

The casting of the stones into the sea provokes the sharpest disagreement about fulfilment. Clarke says it answers to the taking of Tyre by Alexander, who actually took the timbers and stones and rubbish of the old city to fill the space between it and the new, and had to do so before he could take the place; and on the promise that it should be built no more he doubts the whole prophecy refers to the capture by Nebuchadnezzar at all, thinking it may include later conquests down to the sacking of the town in the thirteenth century. Ellicott makes the same move from the grammar: at this verse the nominative changes from Nebuchadnezzar to they, which may intimate that the vision passes again beyond the immediate future to a long succession of calamities. He adds that the spoil is to be understood more of what the Tyrians lost than of what the conquerors gained, since in long sieges the city wasted its substance but generally kept command of the water and sent its moveable wealth away; and he reports a traveller who saw forty or fifty marble columns lying beneath the water in one place. Wesley meets the difficulty of a later Tyre by observing that the town of that name was built on the continent and in propriety of speech was another city.
15:
Henry sets the height against the depth. Tyre was a renowned city, called elsewhere the crowning city because she had crowns in her gift and honoured all she smiled on; she was inhabited of seas, by those who traded at sea and came from all parts bringing the abundance of the seas and the treasures hidden in the sand; and she was strong in the sea, easy of access to friends and inaccessible to enemies, fortified by a wall of water. So she and her people caused their terror to be on all who came there. Those who know their strength, Henry adds, are apt to pride themselves in frightening those they overmatch. And now she is made desolate, no more frequented, with no resort of merchants and none to keep her in repair.

Ellicott is careful about the isles: the word covers not only islands strictly so called but any sea-coast, and the reference here is chiefly to the Mediterranean, though Tyrian commerce reached beyond it. He lists the colonies that looked to Tyre as their mother city and had their high priests from her, in Cyprus and Rhodes and Malta and Spain and Sicily and Africa, adding that even the greatest sent yearly presents home. Gill lays the trembling of the isles partly to the losses their merchants sustained and partly to fear of the same calamities. On the princes Ellicott would say merchant princes rather than actual sovereigns, men raised by commerce to wealth and power, their astonishment described under the figure of eastern mourning; and he would render thrones as seats. Wesley reads the coming down as condolence mixed with fear for their own concerns.

The lament needs two corrections, and Ellicott supplies both. Inhabited of seafaring men should be inhabited from the sea, since the word never means men; the rock of Tyre, built up with dwellings to the water edge, was like a city rising out of the sea. The clause about causing terror has given much trouble; he takes fear as that which causes fear, so that the power of Tyre was so feared that every Tyrian was respected for her sake, as at a later day every Roman carried something of the majesty of Rome about with him. Clarke measures the strength another way, that Alexander despaired of reducing the place unless he could fill the arm of sea between it and the mainland, a work that cost his army seven months.

The descent to the pit closes the oracle, and Ellicott sets a limit on what it claims. Tyre is represented as joining herself to the dead, a striking figure for utter destruction; but this is to be understood of the Tyre that then was, and the question whether there might ever be other inhabitants on that rock does not come within the scope of the vision at all. He also defends the language of the lower parts of the earth: placing the dead below does not prove the writers thought this the actual place of departed spirits, only that human thought must indicate some locality, just as men on opposite sides of the globe all speak of God as above them while knowing that he is everywhere. On the glory set in the land of the living he notes the word is that used elsewhere of Palestine, and reads a promise that when Tyre is forgotten God will establish his people as a living church. Wesley reads it the same way, the beauty and wealth of Israel restored, so that the two captivities end differently. Clarke insists the prophecy must be extended over the entire duration of Tyre, and finds it literally true that no vestige of the old city remains and the ground itself seems washed away; yet he records honestly that Tyre was a place of some consequence long afterwards, with a church in it that became famous.
